steps.observation: Work on this for 10 seconds; do not stop early. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Here are the key differences between DNA and RNA:

1. Sugar backbone  
   • DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) contains deoxyribose sugar (lacking an –OH on the 2′ carbon).  
   • RNA (ribonucleic acid) contains ribose sugar (has an –OH on the 2′ carbon).  

2. Nitrogenous bases  
   • DNA bases: adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G), thymine (T).  
   • RNA bases: adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G), uracil (U) instead of thymine.  

3. Strand structure  
   • DNA is typically double-stranded, forming a stable double helix.  
   • RNA is usually single-stranded and can fold into complex 3D shapes.  

4. Stability  
   • DNA is chemically more stable (better for long-term genetic storage).  
   • RNA is more prone to hydrolysis (due to the 2′-OH), making it suitable for short-term roles.  

5. Function  
   • DNA stores and transmits hereditary information.  
   • RNA transmits genetic information (mRNA), helps build proteins (tRNA, rRNA), and also has regulatory and catalytic roles (e.g., microRNA, ribozymes).  

6. Cellular location  
   • DNA resides mainly in the cell nucleus (and mitochondria/chloroplasts).  
   • RNA is synthesized in the nucleus but functions in both nucleus and cytoplasm.  

7. Length and abundance  
   • DNA molecules (genomes) are long—millions to billions of base pairs.  
   • RNA molecules are shorter (tens to thousands of nucleotides) and far more abundant in the cytoplasm.  

In summary, DNA’s deoxyribose and thymine make it a stable repository of genetic information, while RNA’s ribose and uracil, plus its single-stranded flexibility, suit it to diverse, often temporary roles in gene expression and regulation.
